prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms led to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and opened new regimes of precision measurement and tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B036 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. After the first round I can state the scientific case more sharply, because the chair's first question is the right one. What the lattice clock added to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is a change in the measurement regime and not a refinement. An ion clock interrogates one particle and is limited by quantum projection noise, so the averaging time needed to reach a given uncertainty is very long. The comb made optical frequencies countable, but it did not provide a reference that would hold up under counting. The magic-wavelength lattice lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated with the trap light shift cancelled to first order, so statistical uncertainty and systematic uncertainty improve together. That is why 10^-18 became reachable in hours of averaging and not in months, and why clocks can now be compared across a laboratory or between sites with sub-centimetre gravitational-potential resolution. This is a demonstrated, reproduced result: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE all report uncertainties at the same level, and fibre and free-space comparisons have been made. On the attribution question, my own recollection of the record is that Katori proposed magic-wavelength lattice trapping around 2001-2003 and led the first realisations with Takamoto at RIKEN and Tokyo, while Ye's group made the decisive step to record stability and systematic control and built the many-body-clock and comparison programme that others then followed. Takamoto is a first author of the first demonstration but, as a junior collaborator of Katori, does not displace the proposer; I would treat this as a point to confirm from the archival record before the vote and not as a reason to change names. I also accept the majority view that the pending redefinition of the second is not a condition for recognition. I have therefore moved on that point since round 1. The citation should name the lattice-clock architecture and not a single group's record.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes remains the main reservation, and the colleagues who prefer B022 or B012 are right that the lattice clock is an invention and a measurement tool, and that a large part of its fundamental physics (dark-matter limits, constants, redshift at the millimetre scale) is so far limit-setting and not discovery. Priority is also shared: the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups and the magic-wavelength theory community stand outside a two-name credit, and I cannot verify the full history from the supplied names. Finally I carry the bias of a measurement-tool experimentalist, and the committee should weigh my ranking against members whose first criterion is a new phenomenon in nature. If the committee judges that a prize must reward a new state of matter or a new window on the universe, B036 loses ground, and B022 is then the candidate I would put in front of B012 because the evidence of independent reproduction is stronger for the flat-band phases than for individual neutrino sources.

responses.point: Johansson moved B036 from seventh to first after the opening exchange, and says the nomination's science is persuasive from a device-physics standpoint. He remains uneasy about the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 prizes, which is why the chair asked whether my answer settles his objection.
responses.response: I accept his point on timing and have dropped the idea of waiting for the redefinition of the second; the invention stands on its own reproduced performance. I hope my answer on the overlap helps him: the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions and the 2005 prize rewarded the comb, and neither rewarded a many-atom standard where the trap is removed from the error budget, which is what gives the lattice clock its statistical advantage together with its accuracy. As a fellow member who works on coherence in solid-state systems he will recognise the comparison: this is the difference between demonstrating coherent control of one qubit and making an ensemble useful. Since he moved to B036 after reading the other ballots, I would also ask him to say whether he regards the overlap as outweighed, because a prize built on a reluctant majority is more fragile than one whose supporters agree on why it is novel.

responses.point: Olsson asks the committee to check the archival record of who first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice, in particular the role of Takamoto and the RIKEN team, before the citation is written.
responses.response: I agree that this is the right check and I think we can answer it well enough to decide. As I recall it, Katori's group proposed the idea and published the 2003 and 2005 realisations, with Takamoto the first author on the Nature demonstration, while the JILA group reproduced and then surpassed the accuracy in strontium. I do not read Takamoto's first authorship as a claim equal to Katori's, because the proposal and the programme are Katori's; but I would welcome any member or expert reviewer who can confirm the 2001-2005 sequence from papers and not memory. I also share her view that the redefinition should not hold up the prize, and I note that her own B021 is left as a considered alternative only by her decision, so I do not argue it further.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 on the grounds that it is a new mechanism and not a very large improvement in precision, but says he would be comfortable moving to B036 if the committee weighs maturity above all, and says the incremental case needs to be made.
responses.response: I take the mechanism-versus-precision distinction seriously and would not claim the lattice clock is a new phase of matter. My reply is that a many-atom lattice with a cancelled light shift is a new mechanism for a measurement, and that it has produced results which the earlier technologies could not, for example sub-centimetre redshift resolution. On B022 I agree about elegance and about reproduction across groups, but I weigh the unresolved pairing mechanism and sample-to-sample variation more heavily than he does, and the missing Cao and other first authors make the three-name credit harder to defend today. I take his willingness to move to B036 as the most important sign of convergence in the discussion, and I would ask him to say which finding on twisted graphene would change his mind about timing, which the chair also asked.

responses.point: Eriksson now ranks B022 first, calls B036 a strong but incremental candidate, and argues that moire flat bands are a new platform and should be weighted higher than a refinement of metrology.
responses.response: I agree that a new platform for correlated electrons has more scope as a physical discovery, and I do not dismiss it. My difference is on the evidence at the time of the vote: Eriksson himself lists twist-angle disorder, an open pairing mechanism, the uncredited first authors and earlier band theory as live issues, and he names B036 as the safer choice if interpretation must settle. I would say the word incremental overstates the case, since two orders of magnitude in uncertainty is the sort of step that has opened new measurements; but his point on the redefinition is one I now share, and I have dropped that reservation. If the committee prefers the new-state-of-matter criterion I would not block B022, and it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B012), says the lattice clock is a spectacular improvement of a measurement technology without a new observation of nature, and that its fundamental-physics consequences are still more promise than result.
responses.response: I think this is the strongest challenge and I agree with half of it. The dark-matter, constants and redshift results to date are limits, not detections, and I do not claim otherwise. But a limit that improves by orders of magnitude is a measurement result with consequences, and the redshift test at the millimetre scale has been done, not just proposed. On IceCube I still have the same reservation that he concedes: the diffuse flux is solid, but the source identifications rest largely on IceCube alone and the allocation between Halzen, Spiering, Baikal and DUMAND is contested, and a two-name credit there would leave out much of the lineage. I welcome his statement that he would not object strongly if B036 won, and I have added B012 to my alternatives because he and the chair have made a serious case for it.

uncertainties: Whether the archival record supports Katori for the proposal and first realisation and Ye for record performance as the two credited names, given Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups; I am relying on recollection and would like an expert check.

Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct class of standard and not as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have argued it is distinct but a majority has not yet agreed on how this should be said in a citation.
Whether a committee that weights discovery of new phenomena above new measurement capability would prefer B022, and whether my own tool-oriented outlook biases the weighing.
Whether the 2018 magic-angle experiments will become clearer in the next few years in a way that changes the maturity balance between B022 and B036.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Katori, Ye, JILA, RIKEN or the Tokyo group, so no conflict is apparent for B036. I maintain my declared conflict on B007 (Rempe, Kimble, Lukin): I work on rare-earth-crystal quantum memories and would recuse myself or defer if it advanced; it is no longer part of my preferred configuration or my listed alternatives. My links through the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology to Chalmers and to Goran Johansson bear on B044 and quantum-technology candidates, and would be declared if one of those became the leading proposal.
